content:
Earlier this year, I swapped a gas mower for a robotic mower that can be controlled with an iPhone. Users can manually drive the robot along the edge of the lawn to create a virtual map. Once set up, the robot mows automatically according to a preset schedule.

Recently I've been testing another system called the TerraMow V1000. It uses a completely different navigation method, and after several weeks of testing, I think this machine may be easier for many people to use.

Camera-Assisted Automatic Mapping

The biggest difference between the TerraMow V1000 and the Anthbot M9 I reviewed earlier this year is how each robot understands your lawn.

The Anthbot M9 uses an RTK base station for positioning. During setup, I had to manually drive the mower with my iPhone along the boundary to create the initial map.

The TerraMow V1000 uses what the manufacturer calls the TerraVision 2.0 system. Equipped with three cameras, the mower can automatically map out the lawn area, with no need to lay boundary wires underground or install an additional RTK antenna.

The automatic initial mapping process takes longer, but I think it may be simpler for people who aren't very familiar with computer technology.

To verify this, I asked my mom, who lives in another state, to install and use the TerraMow V1000 on her own without my help. She said everything worked fine. That said, I'm not entirely sure she'd have the patience to first drive the robot around the entire boundary manually with her phone and then mark out all the areas to avoid.

Automatic mapping had a few hiccups in my front yard. There's no fence or other physical barrier between my lawn and my neighbour's, so the TerraMow initially included part of my neighbour's lawn in my map.

I set that area as a no-go zone in the app and the problem was solved. That said, if there's no clearly visible boundary between two lawns, extra care is needed when creating the initial map.

A Peek Through the Mower's Cameras

The TerraMow's cameras also bring one of my favourite features. The iPhone app can show a real-time view of what the mower sees as it works.

During testing, I used my iPhone's screen mirroring feature to keep this view open in a large window on my Mac. I could sit indoors working while watching from the mower's perspective as it moved around the backyard.

This feature isn't strictly necessary for automatic mowing, but it makes the robot more interesting, and sometimes explains why the mower slows down or avoids certain objects. The Anthbot M9 has no equivalent camera view feature.

Beyond that, the two iPhone apps share quite a bit in common. Both support preset schedules, mowing mode adjustments, zone division, no-go zone marking, and remote control of the mower.

TerraMow has one particularly nice variation on that last feature. In addition to traditional left and right virtual joysticks, its app also offers a single-handed joystick mode. You can hold the iPhone normally and steer the mower with your thumb.

Manually driving the mower with an iPhone isn't the main purpose of either system. Ideally, the robot should run automatically according to a preset schedule, with no human intervention. That said, TerraMow's joystick mode is genuinely fun for tidying up small patches the robot missed.

Sometimes I almost feel like I'm controlling the robot with telekinesis (the fun kind). I walk alongside the mower holding the iPhone, give my thumb a slight nudge, and the robot follows my direction.

Every robotic mower app should copy this design.

A More Aggressive Mower

The TerraMow V1000 feels more aggressive than the Anthbot M9. During testing, it cut lower and ran louder.

I wouldn't call the TerraMow "noisy," but the difference is noticeable. The Anthbot runs very quietly—quiet enough that you almost forget it's still running, even when it's mowing at night with its headlights on.

Because TerraMow relies on camera-based navigation, it needs daylight to run reliably. So scheduling daytime mowing becomes all the more important.

The V1000 itself feels solidly built and is also larger than the Anthbot M9. TerraMow includes a protective garage that covers the charging dock, whereas the Anthbot's garage has to be purchased separately.

Most importantly, the TerraMow has been consistently reliable. I relied on it for routine mowing for several weeks in a row, with no human intervention at all.

When Adaptive Mapping Gets Too Clever

The visual intelligence that makes the TerraMow easy to set up can sometimes backfire.

The mower constantly adjusts the map based on what it sees. Each time it finishes a job, saving these changes takes a while, during which you can't perform other operations in the app.

After several days of heavy rain, I ran into an interesting edge case. A puddle had formed somewhere in the yard, and the TerraMow sensibly avoided that area on its next run.

Inside the skipped circular area, the weeds grew taller. Over time, the mower seemed to mistake the growth there for an object to keep avoiding, and even after the ground dried out, that area continued to be skipped.

I used the app's remote control function to drive the mower over manually and cut down the taller grass, and the problem was solved. Once the area returned to normal, automatic mowing resumed there too.

Regular edging can also help the TerraMow approach boundaries more confidently. Tall grass growing along faint boundary lines can otherwise be mistaken for obstacles rather than part of the mowing area.

Anthbot's approach feels less adaptive. It relies more on boundaries and obstacles defined by the user. That method requires more upfront work, but it avoids situations where the map "changes its mind" about the same patch of grass.

9to5Mac Conclusion

Having used both systems, for most people I'd lean toward recommending TerraMow's camera-based approach.

For me, burying wires in the ground is completely impractical, and installing an RTK base station means placing, powering and maintaining extra hardware. TerraMow requires neither.

Its visual navigation isn't flawless. Initial mapping takes longer, unclear property boundaries need manual correction, and its adaptive behaviour once mistook an overgrown patch of grass for a permanent obstacle.

These issues are all manageable. In return, the TerraMow V1000 offers easier setup, reliable automatic mowing, engaging real-time camera views, and the best manual control experience of any robotic mower app I've used.

I genuinely enjoy yard work, but mowing is the most repetitive part. Handing that chore off to a robot frees up time for tending flower beds, edging and detail work, while keeping the lawn tidy.

The TerraMow V1000 excels at this, and I would recommend it, especially for users who want a robotic mower but don't want to bury wires in the ground, install an RTK antenna, or walk around the entire yard with their phone from start to finish.

Amazon currently has the TerraMow V1000 priced at US$999, which is the price after applying a US$200 coupon on the site. The product is also available on TerraMow's official website.
